title: Applied Biomechanics & Human Performance
subtitle: Advanced Hitting, Pitching, Motor Control & Skill Acquisition
standard: Has changing the variable improved performance?
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?

weeks.title: Advanced Biomechanical Foundations
weeks.overview: Functional anatomy and physical capacity, three-dimensional kinematics, kinetics and moments, the kinetic chain, and the foundations of motor control — the physical, mathematical and neuromotor prerequisites for reading pitching and hitting research.
objectives: Distinguish a physical limitation from a coordination strategy or task-specific adaptation.
Interpret 3D joint angles and explain why reported values depend on reference frames and rotation sequences.
Reason quantitatively about forces, moments, impulse, angular momentum and power.
Evaluate kinetic-chain claims, separating mechanical outputs from competitive outcomes.
Explain redundancy, variability and individual movement solutions.

weeks.title: Biomechanical Measurement & Technology
weeks.overview: How human movement is measured — marker-based and markerless capture, force plates, IMUs, EMG, high-speed video and ball and bat tracking — and how to decide whether a measurement is valid, reliable and fit for a specific development decision.
objectives: Explain how each technology produces its outputs and where systematic and random error enter.
Interpret validation and agreement studies, including bias and limits of agreement.
Calculate typical error, ICC-based reliability and minimal detectable change.
Judge whether an observed change exceeds measurement error and within-athlete variability.
Evaluate a vendor claim or biomechanics report before acting on it.

weeks.title: Pitching Biomechanics I — Lower Body & Kinetic Chain
weeks.overview: Phases and events of the delivery, ground reaction forces, pelvis–trunk sequencing, trunk tilt and rotation, and energy-flow analysis — with the correlational evidence read critically.
objectives: Describe lower-body and trunk mechanics and their relationships with ball velocity.
Separate associations with mechanical outputs from demonstrated intervention effects.
Evaluate energy-flow methods and their assumptions.

weeks.title: Pitching Biomechanics II — Upper Extremity & Joint Loading
weeks.overview: Shoulder and elbow kinematics, inverse-dynamics joint moments, load versus tissue capacity, pitch type and velocity effects, EMG, and clinical boundaries.
objectives: Interpret net joint moments without equating them with injury probability.
Weigh evidence on pitch type, velocity and loading.
State clinical boundaries for injury-related questions.

weeks.title: Pitching Biomechanics III — Individualization, Variability & Adaptation
weeks.overview: Individual movement solutions, anthropometric and physical constraints, functional variability, fatigue, and the evidence from intervention trials such as weighted-implement programs.
objectives: Distinguish a kinematic difference from a deficiency.
Evaluate pitching intervention trials critically.
Form individualized, testable development hypotheses.

weeks.title: Hitting Biomechanics I — Rotational Mechanics & Force Production
weeks.overview: Swing phases, ground reaction forces, pelvis–trunk–arm sequencing, segmental angular velocities, joint kinetics and bat acceleration — and the limits of tee-based, cross-sectional designs.
objectives: Explain how force and rotation produce bat speed.
Evaluate the design limits of the hitting biomechanics literature.
Separate mechanical outputs from competitive outcomes.

weeks.title: Hitting Biomechanics II — Bat Path, Contact & Efficiency
weeks.overview: Bat speed, attack angle and swing-path tilt; bat–ball collision physics; contact-point adaptability; what 'mechanical efficiency' can and cannot mean; and the evidence linking swing measures to outcomes.
objectives: Connect bat path and collision physics to contact quality.
Interpret tracking-derived bat metrics and their limits.
Characterize what current evidence links mechanics to competitive outcomes.

weeks.title: Hitting Biomechanics III — Perception, Timing & Adaptability
weeks.overview: Visual limits, gaze and head movement, anticipation and pitch recognition, prospective control of timing, on-line adjustment, and perceptual training and its transfer.
objectives: Explain perception–action coupling in hitting.
Evaluate perceptual-training claims and transfer evidence.
Design representative timing and adaptability tasks.

weeks.title: Motor Control, Coordination & Movement Variability
weeks.overview: Neural control of movement, internal models and optimal feedback control, coordination dynamics, degrees of freedom, and the measurement and meaning of variability.
objectives: Compare major theories of motor control and their practical implications.
Measure and interpret movement variability.
Apply theory to a pitching and a hitting problem.

weeks.title: Advanced Skill Acquisition & Practice Design
weeks.overview: Practice schedule, constraints, feedback, variability, attentional focus and perceptual representativeness treated as distinct design variables, with bias-corrected evidence — building on, not repeating, Course A Week 3.
objectives: Design practice from mechanisms rather than philosophies.
Weigh effect sizes honestly after bias correction.
Distinguish established relationships from illustrative assumptions.

weeks.title: Motor Memory, Retention & Transfer to Competition
weeks.overview: The learning–performance distinction, consolidation and its contested evidence, sensorimotor adaptation, transfer from training to competition, and expertise development.
objectives: Measure durable learning rather than practice performance.
Design retention and transfer tests.
Plan for competitive transfer.

weeks.title: Experimental Design & Intervention Evaluation
weeks.overview: Randomized, crossover and single-case designs; power and the replication problem; causal inference from observational development data; longitudinal within-athlete models; waveform statistics.
objectives: Design and critique intervention studies.
Separate real change from noise and regression to the mean.
Write a pre-registered evaluation plan.

weeks.title: Integrated, Individualized Player Development
weeks.overview: From assessment to competing hypotheses, individualized pitcher and hitter plans, load and readiness decisions within clinical boundaries, and communicating science to players and coaches.
objectives: Turn assessment into individual, testable plans.
Integrate mechanics, physical capacity and motor learning.
Communicate recommendations to players, coaches and executives.

weeks.title: Applied Performance Science Capstone
weeks.overview: The Applied Player Performance Laboratory: two fictional athletes — a pitcher and a hitter — each with a biomechanical assessment, competing explanations, evidence review, individualized hypotheses, intervention, measurement plan, retention and transfer evaluation, risk analysis and executive summary.
objectives: Connect research to actionable, measurable development decisions.
Defend recommendations under uncertainty.
Integrate the semester's science in one applied laboratory.
